stances.claim: Gadon's impeachment complaint against Justice Leonen runs into a doctrinal conundrum: the Sereno decision (May 11, 2018) firmly ruled that QW is proper 'only when the subject act or omission was committed prior to or at the same time of the appointment,' while incumbency acts 'cannot be the subject of a quo warranto proceeding but of impeachment.'

Since Leonen's alleged SALN omissions were committed before his SC appointment (as UP College of Law faculty), the proper remedy is QW, not impeachment -- meaning Gadon may not be able to convince the House or Senate to subpoena Leonen's SALNs, and even if a subpoena issues, the Court may stop subpoenaed officials from complying.

A symmetrical conundrum afflicts Leonen because he dissented in Sereno, opining that QW to oust 'a sitting member of the Supreme Court is a legal abomination... [that] should be overturned in the near future' -- leaving him to choose among (a) asking dismissal based on the very Sereno doctrine he attacked, (b) abandoning his dissent, or (c) saying that despite his dissent, all parties remain bound by Sereno.

Yes, the Supreme Court can halt the House from hearing an invalid or improper impeachment complaint -- Francisco v. House of Representatives (Nov 10, 2003) 'barred' the second impeachment complaint against CJ Davide and 'the House complied even if reluctantly.'

Implicit comparative critique: Corona was ousted by the Senate based on incumbency-period SALN omissions (proper for impeachment); Sereno was ousted by the Court via QW for pre-incumbency SALN omissions -- the two precedents create the procedural template that now defeats Gadon's choice of remedy for Leonen.

notable_anecdotes: The Corona trial backstory: Sen. Franklin M. Drilon 'subtly persuaded' SC clerk of court Enriqueta Vidal to surrender Corona's SALNs from the witness stand, and Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano then 'extracted from the former chief justice... the damning admission that he omitted to declare $2.4 million plus P80 million in his SALNs' -- preserved as the procedural-mechanism explanation of how the Corona conviction was actually engineered.

Reference to Justice Antonio T. Carpio's Dec 10 column already debunking the non-SALN Gadon allegations -- modeling cross-columnist deference and reinforcing CJ's narrow focus on the SALN issue alone.

Sereno doctrine quoted verbatim: QW proper only 'when the subject act or omission was committed prior to or at the same time of the appointment'; incumbency acts 'cannot be the subject of a quo warranto proceeding but of impeachment' -- the precise procedural template that traps Gadon.

Francisco v. House precedent: SC 'barred' the second Davide impeachment and 'the House complied even if reluctantly' -- modeled as institutional-authority precedent for stopping the Leonen impeachment if it proceeds.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the procedural conundrums embedded in Larry Gadon's impeachment complaint against Justice Marvic M. V. F. Leonen -- filed (with the endorsement of Rep. Angelo Marcos Barba and on behalf of Edwin Cordevilla) after the Supreme Court unanimously rejected the prior SALN requests of Gadon and SolGen Jose C. Calida. (CJ limits himself to the SALN issue because Justice Antonio T. Carpio's December 10 column already debunked Gadon's other allegations on Leonen's alleged failure to decide cases on time.) Gadon intends to ask the House Committee on Justice to subpoena the SC clerk of court and the UP registrar for Leonen's SALNs from his 15 years as UP College of Law faculty before his SC appointment. The doctrinal trap: Republic v. Sereno (May 11, 2018, 8-6) ruled that QW is proper 'only when the subject act or omission was committed prior to or at the same time of the appointment,' while incumbency acts 'cannot be the subject of a quo warranto proceeding but of impeachment.' Since Leonen's alleged SALN omissions occurred before his SC appointment, the proper remedy is QW, not impeachment -- meaning Gadon may not be able to convince the House or Senate to subpoena, and even if a subpoena issues, the Court may halt compliance. A symmetrical conundrum afflicts Leonen: he dissented in Sereno, calling QW for sitting justices 'a legal abomination... [that] should be overturned in the near future.' He must now choose among asking dismissal based on the very Sereno doctrine he attacked, abandoning his dissent, or accepting that despite his dissent all parties remain bound by Sereno. CJ also notes that the SC can halt invalid impeachments: Francisco v. House of Representatives (November 10, 2003) 'barred' the second impeachment complaint against CJ Davide, and the House complied 'even if reluctantly.' Comparative context: Corona was Senate-ousted (2012) based on incumbency-period SALN omissions (impeachment-proper), with the SALNs obtained during trial by Sen. Drilon persuading clerk Enriqueta Vidal to surrender them and Sen. Cayetano extracting from Corona himself the 'damning admission' of omitted $2.4 million plus P80 million; Sereno was QW-ousted (2018) for pre-incumbency SALN omissions -- the two precedents create the procedural template that now defeats Gadon's choice of remedy for Leonen.
